Alexander Alesius
ăl-ĕg-zăn´dẽr a-lē´shĭ-ŭs
n. (Alexander Alesius, 1500–1565, Scottish theologian converted by Patrick Hamilton's death, exile and professor at Frankfurt and Leipzig, who argued for the vernacular Scripture against the Scottish bishops)
Latinized from Scots Alane or Aless; he took the name Alesius from Greek alētēs, a wanderer, after his exile.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Alexander Alesius was a canon of St Andrews set to argue Patrick Hamilton out of his opinions, and was converted instead by watching him die. Imprisoned, he escaped to the Continent in 1532 and never safely returned. His first published work answered an edict of the Scottish bishops forbidding the laity to possess the Scriptures in the vernacular; his argument is that the Word was given to the church and not to the clergy, that the people are commanded to search it, and that a bishop who locks it up has usurped what God gave. He taught at Cambridge for a time under Cromwell's patronage, then at Frankfurt an der Oder and Leipzig, wrote commentaries, and kept up a long correspondence with the Scottish reformers from abroad. Joh 20:31 is his ground: “these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.” Rom 15:4 says “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning,” and 2Pe 1:19 calls Scripture “a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place.”

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines the vernacular as belonging to the country of one's birth; native; as, English is our vernacular language.

expand to see more

VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as, English is our vernacular language.

EX'ILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country.

2. The person banished, or expelled from his country by authority.

Key Scripture

Joh 20:31 — "But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name."

Rom 15:4 — "For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope."

2Pe 1:19 — "We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:"

Psa 19:8 — "The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes."

Modern Corruption

A bishops' edict forbidding the people the Scriptures provoked the first Scottish book in their defence, and the argument it makes has never needed revising.

expand to see more

The Scottish prohibition of 1533 is the plainest form of the error: the Word is withheld lest the laity misread it. Alesius's answer is that Scripture itself addresses the people, tells them its purpose, and commands them to search — Joh 20:31 states why it was written and to whom, and Rom 15:4 says it was written “for our learning.” The custodial argument proves too much, since the same reasoning would keep it from the clergy, who have misread it at least as often. The perspicuity of Scripture in what is necessary for salvation is a Reformation doctrine because it is a biblical one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that a Bible in the hand is only half of what Alesius asked for. The withholding now is practical rather than legal: households own several versions and read none, and congregations are fed summaries. 2Pe 1:19 commends the sure word as a lamp for a dark place and adds “whereunto ye do well that ye take heed” — the taking heed being the reader's part. Psa 19:8 promises what follows: “the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek grapho (G1125), to write; didaskalia and didache, learning; phosphoros (G5459), the day star.

Greek grapho (G1125) — to write; John 20:31.

Greek proegraphe, from prographo (G4270) — to write beforehand; Romans 15:4.

Greek didaskalia (G1319) — teaching, learning; Romans 15:4.

Greek bebaios (G949) — sure, firm, steadfast; 2 Peter 1:19.

Hebrew bar (H1249) — pure, clean; Psalm 19:8.

Usage

"“these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ” (Joh 20:31) — the purpose, and the audience."

"“whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning” (Rom 15:4) — written for the people."

"“a more sure word of prophecy” (2Pe 1:19) — the lamp for a dark place."
